summary: Describes a tag for labeling the language of information, how to register values, and how to match tags. It is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 4646 and RFC 4647.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a program can spell-check a document or read it aloud, it has to know which language the document is in. This RFC defines the label, the rules for adding new values to it, and a way to match one label against another.

questions: how to register a language tag
which code should i use for a language
subtitle: How language tags are formed, how to register new ones, and how to match one tag against another.

tldr.problem: Content on the Internet often carries no record of the language it is written in, so tools such as spell-checkers, speech synthesis and Braille output cannot work on it.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is a primary subtag followed by optional subtags joined by hyphens, with the primary subtag drawn from ISO 639 and ISO 639-2 and the first subtag often an ISO 3166 country code. The RFC also defines a language-range construct for matching tags against each other.
tldr.outcome: The tag and the matching rules became a Best Current Practice. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 4646 and RFC 4647.

facts.label: Reserved primary subtags
facts.value: i for IANA registrations, x for private use

today: RFC 3066 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 4646 and RFC 4647, so those are the documents to follow instead. It replaced RFC 1766.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Human beings have used a number of languages, and there are many reasons why one would want to identify the language used when presenting information. In some contexts it is possible to have information available in more than one language, or to provide tools such as dictionaries to assist in the understanding of a language. Many types of information processing also require knowledge of the language in which information is expressed, for example spell-checking, computer-synthesized speech, Braille, or high-quality print renderings.

One means of indicating the language used is to label the information content with an identifier for the language. This document specifies an identifier mechanism, a registration function for values to be used with that identifier mechanism, and a construct for matching against those values.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a program can spell-check a document or read it aloud, it has to know which language the document is in. This RFC defines the label, the rules for adding new values to it, and a way to match one label against another.

sections.title: Language Tag Syntax and Sources
sections.content:
The language tag is composed of one or more parts: a primary language subtag and a possibly empty series of subsequent subtags. The syntax in ABNF is Language-Tag = Primary-subtag *( "-" Subtag ), Primary-subtag = 1*8ALPHA and Subtag = 1*8(ALPHA / DIGIT). The productions ALPHA and DIGIT are imported from RFC 2234 and denote the characters A to Z in either case and the digits from 0 to 9. All tags are to be treated as case insensitive; conventions for capitalisation exist but carry no meaning. ISO 3166 recommends that country codes are capitalised, while ISO 639 recommends that language codes are written in lower case.

The namespace of language tags is administered by IANA. The rules for the primary subtag are that all two-letter subtags are interpreted according to ISO 639, that all three-letter subtags are interpreted according to ISO 639-2, that the value i is reserved for IANA-defined registrations, that the value x is reserved for private use and that its subtags shall not be registered by IANA, and that other values shall not be assigned except by revision of this standard.

For the second subtag, all two-letter subtags are ISO 3166 alpha-2 country codes, tags with second subtags of three to eight letters may be registered with IANA, and tags with one-letter second subtags may not be assigned except by revision. There are no rules apart from the syntactic ones for the third and subsequent subtags. Tags built wholly from assigned codes do not need to be registered with IANA before use.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag is a main part and then optional extra parts, joined with dashes. The main part is one to eight letters, and the extra parts may also contain digits. Capital letters are a convention only and carry no meaning.

sections.title: Choosing a Language Tag
sections.content:
One may occasionally be faced with several possible tags for the same body of text, and interoperability is best served if all users send the same tag and use the same tag for the same language for all documents. If an application has requirements that make the rules inapplicable, the application protocol specification MUST specify how its procedure varies from the one given here.

The RFC then gives rules. Use the most precise tagging known to the sender that can be ascertained and is useful within the application context. When a language has both an ISO 639-1 two-character code and an ISO 639-2 three-character code, you MUST use the tag derived from the two-character code. When a language has no two-character code and the ISO 639-2/T Terminology code and the ISO 639-2/B Bibliographic code differ, you MUST use the Terminology code. When a language has both an IANA-registered tag and a tag derived from an ISO registered code, you MUST use the ISO tag, and the IANA-registered tag SHOULD be deprecated as soon as possible. You SHOULD NOT use the UND (Undetermined) code unless the protocol in use forces you to give a value for the language tag, even if the language is unknown; omitting the tag is preferred. You SHOULD NOT use the MUL (Multiple) tag if the protocol allows you to use multiple languages, as is the case for the Content-Language header.
sections.plainLanguage: When two tags could describe the same text, pick one rule and stick to it. The RFC's rule is to prefer the shortest official code for a language, and to leave the tag out rather than guess when the language is unknown.

sections.title: What a Tag Means
sections.content:
The language tag always defines a language as spoken, written, signed or otherwise signaled by human beings for communication of information to other human beings. Computer languages such as programming languages are explicitly excluded. There is no guaranteed relationship between languages whose tags begin with the same series of subtags; specifically, they are not guaranteed to be mutually intelligible, although it will sometimes be the case that they are.

The relationship between the tag and the information it relates to is defined by the standard describing the context in which it appears. For a single information object, the tag could be taken as the set of languages required for complete comprehension of the object. For an aggregation, such as a document store or a library, it is the set of languages used inside the components. For an object whose purpose is to provide alternatives, the set of tags associated with it is a hint that the content is provided in several languages, and that one has to inspect each alternative to find its language or languages. In markup languages such as HTML and XML, language information can be added to each part of the document identified by the markup structure, including the whole document itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag names a human language, never a programming language. Two tags that start the same do not mean the speakers understand each other. A tag on a set of alternatives says the versions are in several languages, not that one version covers them all.

sections.title: Language Ranges and Matching
sections.content:
Since the publication of RFC 1766, it has become apparent that there is a need to define a term for a set of languages whose tags all begin with the same sequence of subtags. The definition of language-range is derived from HTTP/1.1: language-range = language-tag / "*". A language-range has the same syntax as a language-tag, or is the single character *.

A language-range matches a language-tag if it exactly equals the tag, or if it exactly equals a prefix of the tag such that the first character following the prefix is a hyphen. The special range * matches any tag. A protocol that uses language ranges may specify additional rules about the semantics of *; HTTP/1.1, for instance, specifies that the range * matches only languages not matched by any other range within an Accept-Language header.

The RFC notes that this prefix matching rule does not imply that language tags are assigned to languages in such a way that understanding a language with a certain tag means understanding all languages whose tags begin with that tag. The prefix rule simply allows the use of prefix tags where that is the case.
sections.plainLanguage: A language range is a tag used as a test rather than a label. It matches a tag that is identical to it, or one that starts with it followed by a dash, and the single character star matches anything.

sections.title: Registering New Tags
sections.content:
The procedure in this section MUST be used by anyone who wants a language tag that has no interpretation in chapter 2.2 and has not been registered with IANA. It MAY also be used to register information about a tag that this document already defines. Tags with a first subtag of x need not, and cannot, be registered.

The process starts by filling out the registration form, giving the name and email address of the requester, the tag to be registered, the English name of the language, the native name transcribed into ASCII, a reference to a published description of the language such as a book or an article, and any other relevant information. The form must be sent to the IETF languages list for a two-week review period before it can be submitted to IANA.

When the two weeks have passed, the language tag reviewer, who is appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director, either forwards the request to IANA or rejects it because of significant objections raised on the list. The important thing is that the objection must be made publicly. The applicant is free to modify a rejected application with additional information and submit it again, which restarts the two-week comment period. Decisions made by the reviewer may be appealed to the IESG under the same rules as other IETF decisions. There is no deletion of registrations: when a registered tag should no longer be used, the registration should be amended by adding a remark marking it as deprecated and naming the code to use instead.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new language label, you fill in a form, the list reviews it for two weeks, and a reviewer then sends it on to IANA or turns it down. Anyone who disagrees with the reviewer can appeal to the IESG.

data.title: Language tag
data.code:
Language-Tag = Primary-subtag *( "-" Subtag )
Primary-subtag = 1*8ALPHA
Subtag = 1*8(ALPHA / DIGIT)

viz.caption: WHAT EACH PART OF A TAG CAN MEAN (RFC 3066)

cells: Reserved for private use; IANA does not register its subtags
A country code from ISO 3166 alpha-2
Second subtag, three to eight letters
No rules apart from the syntax

viz.caption: HOW A LANGUAGE RANGE MATCHES A TAG (RFC 3066)

cells: The tag en, and any tag that begins with en-
The tag en-US, and any tag that begins with en-US-
